nameStory: Old field panic grass gets its name from its love of abandoned agricultural fields and disturbed areas where it forms dense colonies. The word 'panic' comes from the Latin 'panicum,' an ancient name for millet and other grain-like grasses. It's nature's way of healing old farmland, moving in quickly when farmers move out!
description: Old field panic grass is a clumping perennial grass that grows 1-3 feet tall in dense tufts. Like other rosette grasses, it has a unique two-season growth pattern - forming low leafy rosettes in fall that overwinter, then sending up flowering stems in late spring. The narrow, pointed leaves are soft green and the delicate seed heads wave gracefully in summer breezes. This adaptable grass thrives in sunny, disturbed areas throughout New England.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms distinctive overwintering rosettes of leaves close to the ground in fall, then sends up separate flowering stems 1-3 feet tall in spring - touch the winter rosettes and they feel surprisingly soft and flexible

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves 2-5 inches long with a soft, almost velvety texture when young - run your finger along the blade and feel how smooth it is compared to rougher grasses

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Airy, open seed heads (panicles) that are 3-6 inches long with tiny, purplish-green flowers that dangle delicately from thin branches - they rustle softly when disturbed

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, slender stems that feel firm but bend easily without breaking - the nodes (joints) are slightly swollen and feel like tiny bumps when you roll the stem between your fingers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny oval seeds less than 2mm long that fall easily when ripe - shake a mature seed head and listen for the gentle patter of seeds hitting the ground

habitat: Old field panic grass thrives in sunny, disturbed areas like abandoned fields, meadows, roadsides, and forest edges throughout New England. It prefers well-drained, sandy or loamy soils and is often found growing alongside goldenrod, asters, and other old-field plants. You'll commonly spot it in areas that were once farmed but have been left to return to nature.

seasonality.spring: Overwintered rosettes begin sending up new flowering stems in May, with fresh green growth emerging rapidly. The contrast between the low rosettes and tall new stems is most obvious now.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs from June through August with delicate, airy seed heads swaying in the breeze. Seeds ripen and begin dropping by late summer, creating the next generation.
seasonality.fall: New rosettes form at the base while old flowering stems turn golden-brown and persist. The rosettes stay green and visible, preparing to survive winter.
seasonality.winter: Distinctive rosettes remain green under snow, while dried flowering stems from the previous year stand like golden sentinels above the snow line.

funFact: This grass is like a botanical time traveler - scientists can study old field panic grass populations to determine when farmland was abandoned because it moves in so predictably during the first stages of forest succession, essentially creating a living timeline of land use history!
confusionNotes: Old field panic grass can be confused with other Dichanthelium species, but the key is looking for those distinctive overwintering rosettes - if you see low, green leaf clusters at the base in fall or early spring, you're likely looking at a rosette grass. Memory trick: 'Rosettes rest through winter' - they're the telltale sign of this genus.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Dichanthelium means 'two flowers' referring to the grass's unique ability to produce two different types of flowers in the same season - showy open ones in summer and hidden cleistogamous (self-pollinating) ones later in the season. This double strategy helps ensure reproductive success even in tough conditions.
compareHints: Among its many Dichanthelium relatives, old field panic grass is distinguished by its preference for truly open, disturbed habitats rather than woodland edges. Unlike deertongue which has much broader leaves, or the various witchgrasses which tend to be more delicate, old field panic grass forms robust clumps and has that classic 'weedy' look of a pioneer species. Its rosettes are also typically more prominent and persistent than most of its cousins.

Starved witchgrass is much more delicate and sparse than its relatives like deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass, which have wider leaves and more robust growth.
Among its many witchgrass relatives, forked witchgrass stands out for its distinctly Y-shaped branching pattern.
Among its Dichanthelium relatives, broad-leaved panic grass stands out for having the widest leaves - most other rosette grasses have much narrower, linear blades.

Among its rosette grass relatives, round-fruited rosette-panicgrass is distinguished primarily by its perfectly spherical seeds - most others like hairy rosette-panicgrass or deertongue have oval or egg-shaped seeds.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, hairy rosette-panicgrass stands out for its consistently fuzzy, velvety texture - most others like deertongue feel smooth or slightly rough.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Bosc's witchgrass tends to have broader leaves than Starved Witchgrass or Slim-leaf Witchgrass, but narrower leaves than broad-leaved panic grass.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, Slim-leaf Witchgrass stands out for having the narrowest leaves - most other Dichanthelium species have broader, more oval-shaped leaves.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, variable witchgrass tends to be more adaptable to different moisture levels than most.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Small-fruited Witchgrass is distinguished primarily by its exceptionally tiny seeds - much smaller than deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass.
Wright's Rosette Grass differs from its relatives like deertongue and the various witchgrasses by forming more perfectly circular, compact rosettes rather than loose clumps.
Compared to its Dichanthelium relatives, slender panic grass is notably more delicate and fine-textured than broad-leaved panic grass, and lacks the dense hairiness of hairy rosette-panicgrass.
Northern witchgrass is distinguished from its Dichanthelium relatives primarily by its northern range preference and smaller overall size.

Among the many panic grass relatives in New England, velvet panicum stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety texture - most other Dichanthelium species are hairy but not nearly as plush-feeling.
Unlike the more common deertongue with its broad leaves and dense shade tolerance, false bearded panic grass has much narrower leaves and prefers wet, open areas.

Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, Heller's rosette grass stands out for its strong preference for partial shade rather than full sun, and its consistently neat rosette growth pattern.

Among the rosette grasses, Scribner's Panicgrass is distinguished by its relatively narrow rosette leaves compared to broad-leaved panic grass, and its more pointed leaf tips compared to the rounded leaves of deertongue.

Eaton's Witchgrass is distinguished from its many Dichanthelium relatives by subtle differences in leaf width, flower cluster branching patterns, and seed size - characteristics that often require expert identification.

Old-field panic grass differs from its many Dichanthelium relatives primarily by habitat preference - while species like deertongue prefer shady woodlands, old-field panic grass seeks out sunny, disturbed areas.
Among New England's rosette grasses, Lindheimer's panicgrass stands out for its nearly hairless leaves and preference for wetter soils.
Hemlock panic grass differs from its Dichanthelium relatives by its preference for coniferous rather than deciduous woods and its particularly delicate, narrow leaves.
